fr:mainmatter.html:p: The deepest connection, and the one you were unsure where to start. The claim: in cubical Agda, a path between two scenes already is an animation, so you may not need to invent the animation category from scratch --- \equiv is an instance of it. This tree builds from a concrete first experiment up to a research frontier, so there is a clear place to begin.

The observation. A path p : a \equiv b carries an interval variable i : \mathbb {I}, and p\, i is "the value at time i." Path concatenation is sequencing animations; \mathsf {transp} and \mathsf {hcomp} are combinators (transport, fill, whisker). So \mathbb {I} is the timeline.

Where to begin (smallest experiment). Pick a structure type with a layout --- say a finite quiver-shaped diagram. Take one equality you can already prove between two such values (a \mathsf {CategorySolver}/ \mathsf {FunctorSolver} output is a ready supply: it proves two morphisms equal). Render it by sampling: evaluate p at i stepped from 0 to 1 in n steps and lay out each sample. If p is a continuous deformation you get a smooth morph; if it is built from discrete rewrites you get the auto-animate steps. That one end-to-end path --- prove, sample, render --- is the whole proof of concept.

Your proofs are the content. The equalities your solvers and hand-written lemmas already establish (two diagram pictures equal, an isotopy of string diagrams, a coherence cell) become animations for free under sampling. You are not authoring motion; you are visualizing proofs you already have.

Directed vs undirected. Two regimes fall out. Undirected (reversible): isotopies, equalities, coherences --- genuine cubical paths, sampled continuously. Directed (irreversible): reduction, functor action --- a morphism in a free category on a rewrite graph (your QuiverPath), rendered as a stepwise trace. Same "sample the interval" renderer, different interval.

The frontier (future work, not v1). Directed type theory (Riehl--Shulman simplicial TT; Max New's directed work) is the directed analog of cubical: a directed interval whose endpoints are asymmetric. It would unify both regimes --- the directed interval as the timeline of an irreversible reduction, its core groupoid as a reversible isotopy --- under one "sample the (directed) interval" renderer. Open questions: does a sampled directed path give well-defined \varphi correspondences at each step? How do \mathsf {hcomp} fillers render (as simultaneous multi-part morphs)? Can naturality (a funExt path) be shown literally as the squares sweeping out? Begin with the undirected sampling experiment above; treat directed TT as the horizon.

The main animation doc stops at Manim parity. This axis goes past it: animating the structured objects of category theory and type theory --- typing derivations, proof trees, commutative diagrams, string diagrams, step-by-step term reduction --- which Manim handles poorly precisely because its primitives are geometric, not structural.

The reframe. Manim's primitives are Mobjects at absolute coordinates: a commutative square is four hand-placed nodes and four hand-placed arrows, with no "square" as an object --- only its picture. Every object we care about is instead combinatorial: a tree of rules, a functor from a free category, a morphism in a monoidal category, an AST plus a rewrite. See the object zoo.

Layout is a functor. Write \mathsf {Layout} : \mathcal {S} \to \mathcal {G} from a category of structures to a category of geometric scenes. A structural morphism S \to S' is transported through \mathsf {Layout} to a geometric morph. Because the picture is generated from the structure, we can emit stable, semantically meaningful data-ids.

Payoff over Tier 1. Manim's TransformMatchingTex heuristically recovers the before/after correspondence from rendered LaTeX, and often guesses wrong. Here the correspondence is a map we already hold, \varphi : \mathsf {elts}(S) \rightharpoonup \mathsf {elts}(S'). Then reveal auto-animate just consumes it: matched ids tween, unmatched in S fade out, unmatched in S' fade in. One engine for proof trees, diagrams, and reductions.

This axis has four parts: the object zoo, how to drive it from existing Agda, the animation category (your "monad / object in a category" guesses, unified), and cubical paths as animations (where your existing equality proofs are the content).

fr:title.text: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The object zoo: structures and their signature animations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each structure on the structure-driven list has a representation we mostly already have in Agda, and a signature animation that is hard or impossible to do structurally in Manim. The recurring engine reduces every case to a partial map \varphi between element-sets plus appear/disappear sets --- exactly what auto-animate consumes.

Typing derivations / proof trees. An inductive tree of rules. Animate: grow bottom-up (proof search, goal to subgoals), cut-elimination as a rewrite, and the substitution lemma as a derivation-to-derivation transform --- a proof of a metatheorem played as an animation.

Categories as arrows / commutative diagrams. A quiver plus a functor from the free category --- you have Free/Category/Quiver and QuiverPath (a morphism is a path of edges). Animate: composition arcing in, a functor action sweeping the whole diagram onto its image, naturality squares filling in, and element-chasing (a dot pushed along arrows until two paths converge).

String diagrams. A morphism in a monoidal category --- you have Categories/Monoidal/Base. Animate: planar isotopy (sliding boxes past each other, the interchange law), yanking/snake equations for adjunctions, and sub-diagram rewriting. This is the one genuinely continuous case: \varphi is a bijection and only positions move, so wires may want true path interpolation (Tier 2).

Step-by-step reduction. An AST plus a rewrite relation; your free CCC normalizer (Free/CartesianClosedCategory/Base) is exactly STLC with reduction. Animate: \beta as substitution = copy the argument subtree to each variable occurrence, with the redex highlighted inside its evaluation context (a one-hole context = a highlighted path to the hole), then the local rewrite.

The shared primitives. highlight, rewrite/replace, copy (substitution, contraction), delete (weakening, cut, yanking), paste (composition), map (functor action), and the lone continuous one, deform (isotopy). All but the last are a partial element-map plus appear/disappear.

fr:title.text: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Agda integration: three pipelines from proof to animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How existing Agda becomes an animation in Forester. The guiding split: Agda owns what (the structure and its transformation), TypeScript/SVG owns how it looks. The structures live in your developments already (see the object zoo); these pipelines move them to the page.

1. Build-time extraction (pragmatic v1). An Agda function \mathsf {toSpec} : \mathsf {Structure} \to \mathsf {AnimationSpec} --- a list of scenes plus the correspondence \varphi --- compiled via Agda's JS or GHC backend and run at build time to emit JSON beside the tree. A \animation{spec-id} macro references it; the theme's JS lays each scene out and lets auto-animate tween between them.

2. Client-side Agda-as-JS (the interactive frontier). Compile the development to JS, ship it, and let the reader type a term that Agda in the browser reduces, playing the animation live. Your free-CCC normalizer becomes a reduction engine on the page. This is past Manim entirely --- the output is not a video but a running evaluator. Aligns with Tier 3 interactivity.
3. Reflection. Use Cubical/Reflection and Tactics/Reflection to quote a term or derivation's AST directly into a spec, avoiding a hand-written \mathsf {toSpec} for the common cases.

What the spec is. A small declarative format: an ordered list of scenes, each a laid-out structure with ided elements, plus per-transition correspondence and timing. It is the value produced by the animation category or its free-monad presentation --- the "description of code input to an animation" made precise.

Open question. Layout itself: do we compute geometry in Agda (portable, but reimplementing tree/quiver/string-diagram layout), or emit only the combinatorial structure and lay out in TS with an existing engine (d3-hierarchy for trees, a quiver layout, a progressive-plane-graph layout for string diagrams)? Leaning TS for layout, Agda for structure and correspondence.

fr:title.text: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: References: projects to raid for Forester animation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: External projects and techniques relevant to the animation design doc.

html:ul.html:li: reveal.js auto-animate --- already in our stack; read their equation auto-animate demo specifically. Drives Tier 0.
Motion Canvas --- the closest "Manim for the web"; steal the live scrubbable-preview idea even if not adopted. Tier 3.
Liqvid --- interactive browser videos, math-friendly. Tier 3.
MathJax v3 --- node-tree access for tagging equation sub-terms. Tier 1.
flubber and GSAP MorphSVG --- arbitrary SVG path interpolation. Tier 2.
Manim Community --- the reference for what we are emulating (TransformMatchingTex, updaters, plotting), even as we reject the imperative model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Structure-driven animation (that axis) --- prior art for animating categorical/type-theoretic objects, not just geometry.

html:ul.html:li: homotopy.io --- the one to study hardest. A proof assistant for finitely-presented n-categories via string diagrams that renders a k-cell as a movie of (k-1)-diagrams: "animation = higher morphism," already shipped in the browser. Heavy overlap with the cubical-paths idea.

DisCoPy --- string diagrams as morphisms in monoidal categories, with functorial semantics, rewriting, and drawing (Python; the type-safety and web stories are where we would improve). Backs the object zoo and the animation category.
AlgebraicJulia (Catlab + AlgebraicRewriting) --- ACSets are the "diagram = functor" representation, with DPO rewriting of diagrams. The structure layer for the zoo.
PLT Redex --- reduction-relation visualization and traces; prior art for term-reduction animations.
Ott, bussproofs, and the prooftrees package (built on LaTeX forest) --- inference-rule and proof-tree typesetting.

Fran / Functional Reactive Animation (Elliott--Hudak) and reanimate --- the denotational \mathsf {Behavior} = \mathsf {Time} \to \mathsf {Scene} model, for the continuous/easing layer alongside the animation category.
